food.text: Taro is one of the most ancient cultivated crops. Austronesian peoples carried it into the Pacific Islands from around 1300 BC, and there it became a staple crop of the Polynesians.

In Ancient Hawaii, which the source dates from 300 AD, Polynesian voyagers brought plants and animals to the islands, including pigs, chickens and dogs. Before cooking, pigs and dogs were killed by strangulation or by holding their nostrils shut, so that the animal's blood was conserved. The settlers also fished, raised taro for poi, and planted coconuts, sugarcane, sweet potatoes and yams, and they cooked meat and fish in earth ovens.

When Polynesian seafarers arrived in Hawaii, few edible plants grew there apart from a few ferns and fruits at higher elevations. Botanists and archaeologists believe the voyagers introduced 27 to more than 30 plants, mainly for food. The most important was taro, which became the main staple of the Hawaiian diet.

Ancient Polynesians sailed the Pacific with pigs, chickens and Polynesian dogs, and introduced them to the islands. In Hawaii, pigs were raised for religious sacrifice, and their meat was offered at altars, with some eaten by priests and the rest eaten in a mass celebration. Pigs and dogs were killed by strangulation or by holding their nostrils shut, so that the animal's blood was kept. The whole animal was then eviscerated, flattened and broiled over hot coals or spitted on sticks.

Early settlers in Hawaii grew kalo (taro), banana, coconut and breadfruit, and raised pigs, chickens and poi dogs. Meat was eaten less often than fruits, vegetables and seafood. Sugarcane served as both a sweet and a medicine, and salt, ground kukui nut and seaweed were popular condiments.

In Hawaiian taro fishponds, fish such as mullet fed on insects and ripe leaf stems of the taro. The taro in turn helped prevent silt by catching it before it went downstream into the ocean. Planting between the wetland areas also provided green manure and medicines.

The early Hawaiian diet may have included as many as 130 different types of seafood and 230 types of sweet potatoes. Some species of land and sea birds were eaten into extinction. The non-native species the settlers brought may also have caused various birds, plants and land snails to go extinct.

art.text: From 1000 BC on, the Lapita people consolidated and began to create the contemporary Polynesian cultures of Samoa, Tonga, and Fiji. From there they ventured further out into the Pacific, carrying their traditions with them.

Starting around 600 BC, works of the Dongson culture of Vietnam, known for their bronze working, can be found in Oceania. Their imagery had a strong influence on the indigenous artistic tradition of the islands.

From about 1000 BC, trade between the Pacific Islands and mainland Asia was growing. This exchange carried objects and imagery across the ocean and helped shape island art long before Europeans arrived.

The artistic traditions of Micronesia, Island Melanesia, and Polynesia descend from later Austronesian voyagers. These voyagers intermixed with native Australo-Melanesians, mostly via the Neolithic Lapita culture.

Lapita people settled the Marquesas and Northern Cook Islands between 200 BC and 1 AD, pushing their culture far out into the Pacific. This was part of the spread that carried artistic traditions to ever more remote islands.
Records of Oceanian art up to 1000 AD remain few. Most artistic traditions, such as New Guinea sculpture, appear to have continued through this period of increasing trade and interaction.

Lapita pottery is almost entirely absent from Eastern Polynesia, where archaeology has so far uncovered only a few shards in the Marquesas Islands. This puzzling gap has shaped debate about how the ancestors of Polynesians travelled.

Because Lapita pottery is so rare in Eastern Polynesia, some researchers suggested the ancestors of Polynesians migrated north via the Philippines and Micronesia. Current data, particularly genetic, instead suggest a long passage through the islands of Melanesia.

literature.text: Polynesian languages descend from Proto-Polynesian, probably spoken in the Tonga and Samoa area around 1000 BC. The myths and legends of the Polynesian peoples were carried in oral traditions, not in writing. Each island group developed distinct but related stories.

Polynesian storytellers told of islands pulled up from the bottom of the sea by a magic fishhook or thrown down from heaven. They also told of voyages, migrations, seductions and battles. The trickster Māui and the demon Ulupoka were widely known, as was the beautiful goddess or ancestress Hina or Sina.

Samoan tradition says many stories and legends were passed on through song, because there was no written language. The pate, a hollowed-out log drum, and the fala, a rolled-up mat beaten with sticks, supplied the rhythms. Dancers added to the beat by clapping their hands.

Proto-Polynesian, the language ancestral to the Polynesian languages, was probably spoken in the Tonga and Samoa area around 1000 BC. The oral traditions of these peoples told of an ancient era called pō and the adventures of gods known as atua, alongside deified ancestors.

In Polynesian oral tradition there is no fixed version of a tale. A story could change within limits according to the setting and the needs of the narrator and audience. Its purpose was to justify and legitimatise the present situation, not to explain the past for its own sake.

Many island groups shared the story of a marriage between Sky and Earth. In the New Zealand version, Rangi and Papa, this union gives birth to the world and all things in it. In some island groups, Tangaroa is of great importance as the god of the sea and of fishing.

Samoan high chiefs recall old voyages in chieftain oratory called lauga, and these voyage accounts are known as taeao. They recount past histories and contacts among the Polynesian islands. Samoans widely believe their islands were the base point for the great voyages of the Polynesian expansion to the East and South.

These Polynesian oral traditions were rich with allegory, metaphor, parable, hyperbole, and personification to recount the exploits of the atua and deified ancestors. Because the accounts were passed on by word of mouth, no single version was fixed, and each retelling could vary with the narrator and audience.

Polynesian traditions were told about the time of "pō" and the adventures of gods called "atua" and deified ancestors. The accounts rely heavily on allegory, metaphor, parable, hyperbole and personification. Each island group also has its own demi-gods and culture heroes, who shade gradually into remembered history.

Because these traditions were only ever spoken, not written, no version was official: narrators could adapt the telling to the setting and the audience. Unlike modern history, which uses knowledge of the past to explain the present, this oral literature instead aimed to justify and legitimize the present situation itself.

Polynesian stories were often tied to geographic or ecological features of the islands. These features could be described as the petrified remains of supernatural beings. In this way the landscape itself served as a reminder of the old tales.

science.text: From 1500 BC onwards, Austronesian navigators from the eastern islands of Indonesia made their way to New Guinea and Melanesia, and then on to the islands of distant Oceania. They were the first people to reach Micronesia and Polynesia.

After the 4th century, Micronesians and Polynesians began to explore the South Pacific. They did not strike out at random. Settlers used their knowledge of wind and water currents to reach their destinations.

Tonga, in western Polynesia, was first settled around 3,300 years ago. It was one of the islands of distant Oceania reached by Austronesian navigators as they spread out from the eastern islands of Indonesia.

According to Schütz, Marquesans colonized the Hawaiian archipelago in roughly 300 CE. They were later followed by waves of seafarers from the Society Islands, Samoa and Tonga, and these Polynesians eventually became the Hawaiian people.

Hawaiian seawater fishponds had canals connected directly to the sea, with a grate of wood and ferns set in the middle. The grates let very small fish enter the pond but stopped bigger, mature fish from leaving.

Hawaiian seawater ponds were enclosed by seawalls of coral or lava rock, ranging from 46 to 1,920 meters long. Builders gathered coralline algae and used it as a natural cement to hold and strengthen the walls.

Radiocarbon dating in Hawaii initially indicated settlement as early as 124 CE. Patrick Vinton Kirch's early books dated the first Polynesian settlements to about 300 CE, with a more recent suggestion of 600 CE. A 2010 study of more reliable samples pointed to about 1219 to 1266 instead.

philosophy.text: Mana was a foundational concept in Melanesian and Polynesian thought: a supernatural force believed to permeate the universe, which any person, object, or place could possess. Rather than being a source of power in itself, mana was seen as an intentional force that could be cultivated or gained.

Tapu was a Polynesian concept of holiness and sacredness carrying an implied prohibition, shaping behavior across societies from the Māori to the Samoan, Tongan, Rapanui, Tahitian, and Hawaiian. Among the Māori, before European contact, it was one of the strongest forces in life, and a violation of tapu could have dire consequences, including the death of the offender through sickness or at the hands of someone affected by the offence. Related forms of the word appear across these cultures, all descending from the reconstructed Proto-Polynesian tapu.

The word mana is reconstructed to Proto-Oceanic, where it likely described powerful forces of nature such as thunder and storm winds, rather than the supernatural. Only as Oceanic-speaking peoples spread eastward across the Pacific did the word's meaning shift toward unseen supernatural power.

The Polynesian word tapu traces back further still, to a reconstructed Proto-Oceanic root tabu, meaning something forbidden and off limits, or sacred, due to a sentiment of awe before spiritual forces. In Hawaii, the same concept survives as kapu, since t and k are interchangeable sounds there.

In Melanesia, animae—the souls of the living, the ghosts of the deceased, and spirits of ghost-like appearance that could imitate people—were believed to act only through mana. These spirits were believed capable of inhabiting other objects, including animals and stones.

culture.text: The Lapita people settled Island Melanesia by sea between about 1600 and 500 BCE. They made dentate-stamped pottery with distinctive geometric designs, closely resembling pottery from the Nagsabaran site in northern Luzon. They are the direct ancestors of the Austronesian peoples of Polynesia, eastern Micronesia and Island Melanesia.

Austronesian navigators reached New Guinea and Melanesia from 1500 BC onwards, then pushed on to the islands of distant Oceania. They were the first to reach Micronesia and Polynesia. Tonga, in western Polynesia, was first settled around 3,300 years ago.

In 2003, a large cemetery was discovered at Teouma on Efate Island in Vanuatu, with 25 graves holding burial jars and 36 human skeletons. All the skeletons were headless: at some point after the bodies had been buried, the skulls had been removed and replaced with rings made from cone shells, and the heads had been reburied. One grave held the skeleton of an elderly man with three skulls sitting on his chest, and another held a burial jar depicting four birds looking into the jar. Carbon dating of the shells placed the cemetery in use around 1000 BCE.

Within three or four centuries, between about 1300 and 900 BC, the Lapita culture spread 6000 km east of the Bismarck Archipelago. It reached as far as Fiji, Samoa and Tonga, carrying its tradition of pressed-pattern pottery with it.

Within three or four centuries, between about 1300 and 900 BCE, Lapita culture spread 6000 km east from the Bismarck Archipelago to Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. Its large permanent villages stood on beach terraces along the coasts. In this region the distinctive Polynesian culture then developed.

The name Lapita comes from a 1952 excavation in New Caledonia, where archaeologists mishearing the Haveke word xapeta'a, meaning 'to dig a hole', coined the term. The type site is on the Foué peninsula, and the settlement and pottery sherds were later dated to 800 BCE. More than 200 Lapita sites have since been found.

The Samoan Islands may have been settled some time before 1000 BC, according to the natives' own suggestion. Many Samoans also widely believe that the islands were the central base point for the great voyages of the Polynesian expansion to the East and South.

The Mana skeleton is a complete skeleton of a Lapita woman who lived in Fiji in 800 BCE. When her face was reconstructed with computer modelling, her features resembled those associated with Polynesian, Fijian and Asian ancestry, yet she did not clearly align with any one of these groups.

The Marquesas Islands were colonized by seafaring Polynesians as early as 300 AD, thought to have come from Tonga and the Samoan Islands. The dense population lived in the narrow valleys and consisted of warring tribes.

Estuaries and streams were adapted into fishponds by early Polynesian settlers in Hawaii as long ago as 500 CE or earlier. Packed earth and cut stone were used to create habitat, making ancient Hawaiian aquaculture among the most advanced of the original peoples of the Pacific.

At Teouma on Efate Island in Vanuatu, a large cemetery was found in 2003, with 25 graves containing burial jars and a total of 36 human skeletons. All the skeletons were headless: at some point after the bodies were first buried, the skulls had been removed and replaced with rings made from cone shells, and the heads had been reburied. One grave held the skeleton of an elderly man with three skulls sitting on his chest, and another held a burial jar depicting four birds looking into the jar. Carbon dating of the shells placed the cemetery in use around 1000 BCE.

In Western Polynesia, Lapita pottery grew less decorative and progressively simpler over time. It seems to have stopped being produced altogether in Samoa by about 2,800 years ago, and in Tonga by about 2,000 years ago.

Dating of the first Polynesian arrival in Hawaii has shifted over time. Radiocarbon dating initially indicated a possible settlement as early as 124 CE, and Patrick Vinton Kirch's early books placed the first settlements at about 300 CE, with later suggestions of 600 CE.
